articles.title: Demand for Christmas donations up, Somerset charities say
articles.summary: Charities collecting Christmas presents for struggling families say demand has gone up.
articles.body:
Charities giving Christmas presents to struggling families say more children need their help - but they are getting fewer donations this year.

The Chard Christmas Present Appeal said it was having to deal with a high-than-normal demand this year, and blamed the problem on more people struggling financially.

Martyna Lee, founder of the appeal, said a lot of families were worried about affording presents for their children due to the cost of living crisis and have "tears in their eyes" when the charity can help them.

She added: "We are getting more referrals and less donations because of cost of living, so we do struggle. Cost of living is going to get harder and harder."

Song urges builders to talk about mental health

MP facing voice loss after surgery shows recovery signs

Bid launched for 410 new homes near motorway

Lee started the appeal by herself in 2019 from her living room as part of the Lord's Larder food bank in Chard.

They rely completely on donations and do not receive any funding.

"With one family, the social worker asked the children what they would like for Christmas and they asked for pencils and a colouring book," Lee said.

"That broke my heart. They weren't asking for expensive gifts.

"So I made sure they had a large gift package, including board games."

She added that another family she remembers had a fire at their home just before Christmas and they lost "nearly everything".

"We managed to get them fantastic gifts and a Christmas tree and decorations," Lee said.

Meanwhile, Taunton's charity appeal Christmas Sparkle said their demand has risen sharply over the last couple of years, with 500 presents given out in 2015 to 10,000 last year.

They said they are expecting even higher demand this year.

Gill Harrison, founder and manager at Christmas Sparkle, said she believes the cost of living crisis is increasing the demand for their services.

"When we started the project in 2015, we gave out 500 individual gifts. Last year, it was around 2,300 parcels, that's about 10,000 individual gifts," Harrison said.

"We are expecting possibly even more requests this year. That's mostly because of the cost-of-living crisis."

Harrison said they work with schools, social services, police, women's refuges and community nursing teams, which have all increased their referrals to Christmas Sparkle over the last few years.

articles.title: Builder's song encourages workers to talk about mental health
articles.summary: A Somerset builder has written a song to raise awareness and money for mental health charities.
articles.body:
A construction company manager is using music as a way of getting more men in the industry talking about their mental health following the loss of his uncle.

Ben Francis, from Bruton, Somerset, has written a song as a way of raising awareness and money for mental health charities after his uncle, Jonathan Carpenter, took his own life in December 2023.

Jonathan was a "meticulous carpenter" and Francis hopes his uncle's story and his song will strike a cord with fellow construction workers and encourage them to open up about their mental health.

"I want natural construction voices to come and be heard and help me share the message that we should be talking about mental health in construction."

Christmas donations gift demand up, charities say

MP facing voice loss after surgery shows recovery signs

Bid launched for 410 new homes near motorway

"It takes a little bit of strength to say how you're feeling, so think of it as a good thing," he said.

"In the industry we haven't done it and mental health awareness has been around for while now and what I want to do is take a bit more action."

Francis has worked in the industry since 15 and now runs his family business.

Construction sites are well known for their banter and camaraderie but Francis believes that sometimes things might not be all as they seem.

"[It was] a terrible moment because [my uncle] felt like he couldn't reach out and talk about how he was feeling," he said.

"Even for the guys who might have had an inkling, no one really knew how to deal with what was going on.

"I think he was struggling personally, he was going through what a lot of guys go through, he was 50 and sort of in a mid-life crisis moment and unsure of what he was doing.

"He had lost a lot of confidence in what he was doing and I think all these things snowballed."

Studies have shown that talking and being part of an active community can help improve overall mental health and Francis hopes that introducing this to construction could go a long way.

"If you ask guys on site how they're doing, the common phrase is 'living the dream' and we all know that's sarcasm," he said.

"I think that each day the pulling pranks and joking is just a way of dealing with issues in their own way but actually they're not speaking to anybody.

"We should be talking on site and just being able to open up about our feelings."

Jonathan was a keen musician and started creating music at a very young age.

He passed this love of music on to his nephew and helped him write his first song at just 10 years old.

Francis has now released a new single called Smile in the Dirt, that highlights the pressures of working in the industry and calls on people to talk about how they are feeling.

The song was recorded at Abbey Road Studios and all proceeds will go to four mental health charities.

articles.title: Shadowy Indian election ‘consultants’ add US midterms to global footprint
articles.summary: India’s election consultants are exporting covert campaign tactics to manipulate elections worldwide, including the US.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India — In an unfurnished flat in a nondescript Ahmedabad neighbourhood in western India, a 22-year-old digital content creator worked through the nights, designing posters and editing videos for a presidential campaign thousands of kilometres away — William Ruto’s 2022 bid for the presidency in Kenya.

Rajan Kumar’s content was not shared by Ruto’s official campaign. Instead, the 50 social media posts he created for $7 a day were shared on shadow social media accounts that conceal their identity to make coordinated messaging appear independent while backing Ruto’s campaign.

For content, Kumar said he would trim opposing leaders’ speeches or interviews to twist their statements, or create posters with false claims amplifying Ruto’s prospects and popularity ahead of the election.

“If there’s a woman politician, we simply link her to someone to damage her reputation. It’s one of the easiest ways to discredit,” Kumar told Al Jazeera, adding that “all controversial content” is diverted to shadow pages for “extensive distribution”.

Ruto won the 2022 election and became Kenya’s fifth president.

Four years later, as the United States heads into its midterm elections on Tuesday, researchers have found that Indian social media bots and accounts have been shadow-posting videos backing specific campaigns. The New York Times first reported such posts supporting US Democratic politician Haley Stevens ahead of the August 4 Senate primary in Michigan, which she lost to Abdul El-Sayed, the party’s candidate for the midterm election.

But the US is only the latest theatre of electoral war where politicians are banking on Indian social media mercenaries-for-hire, who have fought shadow election campaigns in several countries in South America and Africa.

Nearly a dozen political consultants in India, who spoke with Al Jazeera for this report, say there are no limits, guardrails, or red lines in such shadow campaigns.

“We are manipulating elections; there is no other way to say it,” said Tushar Giri, a political consultant in New Delhi. “The concept of electoral democracy is so overrated. There is no free will for voters. Everything is manipulated.”

Political consultancies advise politicians and election campaigns on how to win public support and elections. Such specialised private companies selling political persuasion as a service emerged in the US in the 1930s.

With the boom in social media, dirty tricks have spread to online platforms to manipulate and attract voters, especially by running targeted advertising campaigns on Meta and Google platforms to reach millions of voters. Previous reports have found that Russia used similar tactics to influence voters in the US, for instance.

Strategies for dissemination of content deemed too controversial for official accounts during election campaigns vary, ranging from political consultancies taking over a party’s established shadow pages on Meta or Google to making new ones from scratch, rebranding existing pages to suit a campaign’s needs, or opting for pages for hire.

An Al Jazeera investigation in the run-up to India’s 2024 national election revealed a sprawling network of such shadowy pages on Meta and Google products like Facebook, Instagram and YouTube on sale — skirting the platforms’ policies against such misuse of targeted advertisements to influence voters.

Antibot4Navalny, an anonymous group of disinformation researchers that investigates and exposes coordinated online influence operations, particularly those linked to Russia, told Al Jazeera that it found at least 28 such accounts on X (formerly Twitter) sharing videos supporting Stevens’s campaign in the Democratic primary in Michigan, garnering more than seven million views.

At least 15 of the identified accounts were posting from India, a review by Al Jazeera has found.

Researchers at Clemson University’s Media Forensic Hub have also identified similar tactics being used by for-hire Indian accounts and pages to support Stevens’s campaign against El-Sayed.

Amogh Dhar Sharma, author of Backstage of Democracy — a book on Indian political consultancies’ workings, said politicians like to keep voters’ focus ahead of elections “on things that happen in the public eye”.

“But sometimes the real power is being wielded, completely hidden from the public eye,” Sharma told Al Jazeera, referring to political consultancies. “The way it creates certain, hidden sources of power in a democracy is one of the biggest ethical concerns.”

In India, such political consultancies now make up the backbone of any election campaign, and their work serves as marketing material to lure politicians in other countries.

“We have a proven track record of delivering desired results in a complicated electoral democracy like India, which now attracts foreign campaigns too,” said Giri, the New Delhi-based consultant.

Rules set by Meta, Facebook’s parent firm, disallow users from any “attempt to or successfully sell, buy, or exchange” accounts, or from operating under false or stolen identities. In general, both Meta and Google’s policies require political advertisers to verify their identities and disclose who paid for election advertisements, though specific rules vary from country to country.

But Indian consultants tell Al Jazeera that these community standards are routinely violated.

“These platforms have long pages of such rules, but when you read between the lines, there are several loopholes one can exploit,” said Giri. Premium virtual private networks (VPNs) are the go-to tools for such consultancies when they face restrictions in one geography. Sometimes, changing an account’s country of origin simply does the job, enabling a person sitting in a foreign country to run targeted political advertisements.

Giri recalled meeting representatives of a presidential campaign in Suriname last year, although negotiations ultimately fell through. Sharma, the author, told Al Jazeera that he found Indian consultancies working in Australia and Germany as well during his research. Consultants told Al Jazeera that they have similarly worked on campaigns in India’s neighbouring countries, including Nepal and Sri Lanka.

Kumar, who worked for Ruto’s campaign for the Kenyan presidency in 2022, said he was paid about $7 a day under a monthly contract and was asked to deliver up to 100 creatives on some days, coordinated via groups on Telegram.

He said he never worked directly with any of Ruto’s representatives, and that content creators like him are never informed of the identities of all the individuals involved in the supply chain that leads up to senior officials in a campaign.

“One always needs to be careful and hide footprints nonetheless,” he said. Chats are deleted, and SIM cards are destroyed frequently.

Two Indian political consultants, Zulfiqar Ahmad Khan and Mohamed Zaid Sami Kidwai, who were working for Ruto’s campaign, went missing in Nairobi in July 2022 ahead of the election. They were found dead in October, allegedly abducted by an elite police unit in Kenya. After winning, Ruto disbanded that unit. Fifteen officers were accused of murder, but in August 2026, Kenya’s High Court terminated those charges after the prosecution requested that the murder investigation be discontinued.

The shadowy nature of the work that consultants like Kumar do extends to payments, several political consultants explained.

“Black money is a pillar of political consultation,” one consultant told Al Jazeera, requesting anonymity, fearing for their safety. “We have companies abroad that hire a person on paper for random work to make payments, but it is just a front to funnel money.”

Several consultancies rely on hawala networks — an informal, trust-based money-transfer system that allows people to send funds across borders through brokers, bypassing conventional banking channels.

At least three consultants identified export-focused businesses in Old Delhi’s sprawling Chandni Chowk market in the national capital territory as one such hub. A consultant who spoke with Al Jazeera for this report on condition of anonymity recalled a dramatic business deal two years ago.

The consultant carried an Indian banknote bearing a specific serial number, which served as a code to identify and collect the payment. “I saw people use 10-rupee notes to collect millions in cash,” they told Al Jazeera. “It was like I’m in a movie.” They refused to disclose the country or campaign that paid for this particular transaction.

Giri, the consultant, told Al Jazeera that in the last couple of years, India has turned into “a big wholesale market to run these shadow political campaigns”.

“It is like you buy toys from China; similarly, you can manipulate elections anywhere in the world at the cheapest cost in India,” he said.

Author Sharma had a similar analogy to explain the nature of India’s political consultancies.

“This is perhaps an extension of the global outsourcing industry that has been central to India’s economic growth,” Sharma argued. “Just as India became a hub for business-process outsourcing in the 2000s”, the country is now seeing the rise of political consultancies that campaigns can hire to outsource their less transparent operations.

Sharma added that the physical distance of those behind these shadowy social media promotions and the campaigns they work for gives everyone involved “plausible deniability” if operations are revealed.

Giri, the consultant, argued that what makes consultants successful is how far they are willing to go to help a campaign.

“What are the limits? If one agency can execute filthy tricks to manipulate a voter — and think beyond the political party’s own imagination — they are rewarded accordingly,” he said. “The dirtier you can get, the more money and opportunities there are.”

articles.title: In 1917, a Utah businessman found that transporting bricks by road was too expensive; he sent them through the postal system instead, until the sheer volume forced the US government to intervene
articles.summary: In the early days of America's Parcel Post system it seemed everything that could fit within the rules was fair game for delivery.
articles.body: In the early days of America's Parcel Post system it seemed everything that could fit within the rules was fair game for delivery. Farmers sent crops, families sent food and household goods, and businesses soon discovered that the postal network could be an unexpectedly cheap alternative to traditional freight. But in Utah, one businessman took the idea much further and used the mail to ship thousands of bricks for an entire bank.When the postal service was a shipping networkAccording to the Smithsonian National Postal Museum, on January 1, 1913, Parcel Post officially began, changing the way Americans could ship items. The service was particularly popular with rural families who had to haul goods into towns with express offices before they could be sent on. The new system linked packages straight to rural mailboxes, and it was nearly instantly popular. In the first half of the year, some 300 million parcels were processed. The weight limits increased quickly, from 11 pounds to 20 pounds, then eventually 50 pounds.The service was not limited to normal household parcels. Eggs, butter, vegetables and other common commodities were regularly sent through the mail, and the need for specially designed packaging arose.A cheaper way to build a bankA report by the Medium states that in 1916, William Horace Coltharp, who had helped build the Bank of Vernal in Utah, had a strange transportation problem. The decorative pressed bricks he wanted were made by the Salt Lake Pressed Brick Company, which was about 125 miles away in a straight line. However, in the mountainous landscape, conventional transport was much more complicated. Medium reports that shipping the bricks by normal freight routes would cost more than four times their value. Coltharp looked to Parcel Post as a cheaper alternative.Postal rates were determined by the actual distance between places not the much longer route freight had to travel. Coltharp used the difference to have individual bricks wrapped and packed in boxes of about 50 pounds each, for mailing.The post office starts to strainWhat started as a brilliant way to save money quickly became a logistical nightmare. Thousands of bricks started arriving at Vernal, and the local postal operation was overwhelmed.In the end, Coltharp sent about 15,000 bricks, for a total shipment of some 37.5 tons, or 75,000 pounds, according to Medium. At the height of construction, the Vernal post office was already handling some two tons of mail daily, so the brick deliveries were particularly taxing.The Smithsonian National Postal Museum estimates the shipment weighed 40 tons, and Salt Lake City and Vernal postmasters and the Uintah Railroad, which hauled the parcels, were overwhelmed by the deliveries.A new rule closes the loopholeUltimately, the extraordinary shipment forced federal officials to rethink how Parcel Post could be used. The Post Office Department ruled that no one sender could send more than 200 pounds of parcels to one recipient in a single day.But by then Coltharp’s unconventional approach to building had already served its purpose. The bricks were sent from Salt Lake City to Vernal, piece by piece, by postal service.The episode became one of the most memorable illustrations of how a new public service could be stretched far beyond its intended purpose, and how quickly an inventive shortcut could expose the limits of the system itself.Images Courtesy: Smithsonian National Postal Museum and isockYou use AI every day. articles.title: Lady Gaga and her mother built a youth mental-health foundation; by May 2026, more than 100,000 people worldwide had earned certificates through its programme teaching how to support someone in distress
articles.summary: Pop star Lady Gaga and her mother, Cynthia Germanotta, have spent more than a decade working to make mental-health support more accessible to young people.
articles.body: Pop star Lady Gaga and her mother, Cynthia Germanotta, have spent more than a decade working to make mental-health support more accessible to young people. Their efforts reached a new milestone in May 2026, when the Born This Way Foundation announced that more than 100,000 Be There Certificates had been earned worldwide through a free online programme teaching people how to support someone struggling with their mental health.The foundation, co-founded by Gaga and Germanotta in 2012, marked the achievement in partnership with Canadian youth mental-health organisation Jack.org. The certificate programme teaches participants how to recognise signs of distress, respond with care and help someone connect with appropriate support. The foundation announced the milestone on May 31, 2026, and linked it to its Generation Be There campaign, which aims to equip young people with practical skills to support themselves and others.According to the foundation’s official impact timeline, the campaign had 186 partner organisations and attracted more than 590 attendees across its events. The initiative focuses on turning conversations about mental health into practical action, encouraging people to become more confident in supporting friends, family members and peers who may be struggling.How Lady Gaga and her mother started the foundationThe Born This Way Foundation was announced in January 2012 and officially launched on February 29 that year at Harvard University. The initiative grew out of Gaga’s interest in building a kinder, more accepting environment for young people, particularly those facing bullying, social pressure and difficulties with self-confidence.In the announcement published by Harvard Graduate School of Education, Germanotta said the foundation grew from her daughter’s desire to create a world in which people were accepted for who they were, regardless of their differences. She also spoke about the lasting effects young people can experience when they do not receive adequate support. The foundation initially focused on issues including wellbeing, anti-bullying, mentoring, self-confidence and youth empowerment. It brought together researchers, charitable organisations and young people to explore ways to encourage acceptance and create safer environments.Over time, mental-health awareness and support became central to its work. Rather than relying only on public awareness campaigns, the organisation developed initiatives intended to give young people tools they could use in everyday situations.What is the Be There Certificate?The Be There Certificate is a free, self-paced online mental-health course created by Jack.org in partnership with Born This Way Foundation. It is available in English, French and Spanish and is designed to help people support someone who may be experiencing mental-health difficulties. The course centres on five principles, known as the Be There Golden Rules: “Say What You See”, “Show You Care”, “Hear Them Out”, “Know Your Role” and “Connect to Help”.The first encourages people to describe changes they have noticed without making assumptions about what someone is experiencing. The second focuses on expressing concern and showing that the person matters. Listening without judgement is another central element, alongside understanding the limits of one's role and helping someone access further support when necessary.The programme also stresses that supporting someone does not mean taking responsibility for solving all their problems. Instead, it aims to help participants recognise when a person may be struggling, respond appropriately and connect them with relevant resources. The course is educational rather than a professional qualification in mental-health care. Completing it does not make someone a therapist or replace professional assessment and treatment. Its purpose is to help ordinary people feel better equipped to offer safe, informed support.From awareness to practical actionThe 100,000-certificate milestone represents the reach of a programme that seeks to make mental-health support a shared responsibility rather than something left exclusively to professionals. In April 2026, Born This Way Foundation launched its Generation Be There campaign to expand participation and encourage more people to complete the course. The campaign works with organisations and community partners to bring the programme to young people and the adults who support them.The foundation’s impact timeline said the initiative had more than 186 partners and over 590 attendees across campaign events as it reached the 100,000-certificate milestone. Its activities included events, discussions and outreach designed to encourage people to move beyond simply discussing mental health and learn practical ways to help. The course has also received recognition from the digital and communications industries. The foundation lists the Be There Certificate among the recipients of a 2023 Gold Anthem Award, a 2023 Shorty Award and a 2023 Webby Honoree distinction.Why everyday support mattersThe initiative reflects a broader approach to youth wellbeing: building communities in which people feel comfortable discussing mental-health struggles and seeking help. Friends, classmates, colleagues and family members may notice changes in someone's behaviour before that person approaches a professional, making informed and compassionate responses important. articles.title: Big Aatmanirbhar push: Defence ministry inks Rs 53,866cr contract with GRSE & GSL for 8 next-generation corvettes for Navy
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In a big push to self-reliance in warship manufacturing, the defence ministry on Monday signed contracts worth Rs 53,866.5 crore with two
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a big push to self-reliance in warship manufacturing, the defence ministry on Monday signed contracts worth Rs 53,866.5 crore with two shipyards — Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers Limited (GRSE) and Goa Shipyard Limited (GSL) — for the acquisition of eight next generation corvettes (NGCs) for the Indian Navy. Under the contracts, GRSE will construct five corvettes, while GSL will construct the remaining three.The project marks a significant milestone in India's indigenous warship design and construction capabilities, as it is the first project in which the ships will be indigenously designed by the Indian Navy and constructed by defence public sector undertakings (DPSUs) selected through a competitive process. The contracts were inked in the presence of defence secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh.A corvette in the Indian Navy is a small, fast and heavily-armed warship ranked just below a frigate in size. Such agile warships are meant for anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare and coastal defence. They perform maritime surveillance, search-and-attack operations, escort duties for larger fleet ships, and patrol missions. The Indian Navy currently operates 18 to 24 corvettes in active service.The NGCs will be equipped with state-of-the-art capabilities, including advanced missiles, weapons and sensor suites, enabling them to undertake missions across the air, surface and sub-surface domains, a defence ministry’s release said.Welcoming the move, defence minister Rajnath Singh posted on X, “Great news for India’s indigenous shipbuilding ecosystem. The NGC project for the Indian Navy will provide a significant impetus to India’s shipbuilding sector by strengthening collaboration among DPSUs, private shipyards and Indian industrial partners, including MSMEs. The construction of these ships will generate approximately 72 lakh person-days of employment in the shipyards and 460 lakh person-days in ancillary industries and MSMEs over the next 10 years.”“By promoting the use of made-in-India materials and equipment, indigenous technologies, and Indian skills and expertise, the project represents a major step towards achieving Aatmanirbharta in defence manufacturing and reinforces PM Shri Narendra Modi’s commitment to make in India,” he further posted.The induction of these ships will significantly enhance the Indian Navy’s operational capabilities in safeguarding maritime trade routes, conducting anti-surface and anti-submarine warfare operations, strengthening coastal defence, undertaking littoral combat operations, and carrying out maritime presence and surveillance missions.

articles.title: A woman who came to Kentucky on a fiance visa signed a prenup 11 days after arriving; her husband disclosed assets above $1 million versus her $39,000, and an appeals court upheld the agreement after their divorce
articles.summary: A woman who moved from China to Kentucky on a fiance visa and signed a prenuptial agreement just 11 days after arriving in the United States has lost her
articles.body: A woman who moved from China to Kentucky on a fiance visa and signed a prenuptial agreement just 11 days after arriving in the United States has lost her attempt to overturn the agreement following her divorce.Yuancong Zhang challenged the agreement with her former husband, Stuart M Chen, whose disclosed assets exceeded $1 million, compared with her approximately $39,000. Zhang argued that she had signed the document under pressure and did not fully understand its terms because of her limited English.However, the Kentucky Court of Appeals upheld the agreement on Friday, finding no reason to overturn the family court's earlier decision.According to the judgment, the couple met in 2008, when Zhang lived in China. After several years together, they decided to marry. Before the wedding, Chen hired a lawyer in Kentucky to prepare an agreement that would protect his property for his two children. One of his children was permanently disabled and required lifelong care.The agreement stated that both Zhang and Chen would keep the property they owned before marriage, along with any property later acquired in their individual names. It also prevented either spouse from claiming a share in the increase in value of the other's property, financial support after divorce or certain benefits following the other's death.Chen gave Zhang the document in January 2015, months before she travelled to the United States. According to court records, he advised her on at least three occasions to have it translated into Chinese and explained it to her. Zhang arrived in Kentucky in July 2015, signed the agreement 11 days later and married Chen that September.Why Zhang challenged the agreementThe marriage continued until 2023, when Chen filed for divorce and asked the court to enforce the prenuptial agreement. Zhang opposed it, arguing that the circumstances in which she signed the document were unfair and that enforcing it would leave her struggling financially.At a hearing in April 2024, Zhang said the agreement had been presented to her in English, a language in which she was not proficient. She argued that Chen had failed to provide a Chinese translation or arrange legal representation for her.She also pointed to her immigration situation. Zhang had entered the country on a K-1 fiance visa, which required her to marry Chen within 90 days or return to China. She claimed that because the marriage depended on signing the agreement, she had little meaningful choice.Her financial position had also changed after moving to the United States. Before marriage, Zhang had worked as a journalist in China for 16 years. She was 46 at the time and, according to her testimony, had been four years away from qualifying for retirement there.Zhang did not work during the marriage until Chen filed for divorce. She told the court that her long absence from employment and limited English made finding work difficult. She eventually secured a part-time supermarket job paying approximately $100 a week and said she was applying for public assistance.Why court rejected her argumentsThe Madison Family Court ruled in October 2024 that the agreement was valid and enforceable. It subsequently applied the agreement when granting the divorce in December that year.Zhang appealed, but the appeals court agreed with the earlier decision. It noted that she had received the document approximately six months before signing it and had been repeatedly advised to seek a translation or explanation.The judges said the family court had found that Zhang had sufficient time, resources and ability to obtain help understanding the agreement but had chosen not to do so.The court also rejected her argument that making the marriage conditional on signing the agreement amounted to unlawful pressure. It explained that prenuptial agreements are permitted under Kentucky law and that insisting on such an agreement before marriage did not, by itself, establish duress.Another issue was whether Zhang should receive financial support after divorce. She argued that her age, limited English and employment difficulties meant she could not adequately support herself.However, the court found that the financial difference between the couple had existed when they married and had not materially changed during their relationship.What judges said about her financial situationThe family court had found that Chen was retired, supported his disabled adult son and lived on his retirement assets. Zhang had a journalism degree, had recently begun working and still appeared to have some savings in China.Although Zhang claimed she had been homeless for a period after separation, the court noted that Chen had allowed her to return to his home and supported her until she found employment and an apartment.The appeals court also pointed out that Chen had signed a financial sponsorship declaration during Zhang's visa process. That obligation was separate from the prenuptial agreement, and Zhang appeared to retain the option of pursuing it through another legal action.The judges acknowledged that they might have reached a different conclusion themselves, but said the family court's findings were supported by sufficient evidence. The October 30 ruling therefore left both the prenuptial agreement and the divorce decree in place.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ryanair says it may freeze workers' pay and raise airfares
articles.summary: The airline says fuel prices may rise by €2bn in 2028 unless there is an end to the US-Israel war with Iran.
articles.body:
Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff and confirmed airfares will be "materially higher" next summer because of a sharp rise in fuel costs following the US-Israel war with Iran.

The airline said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict.

Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be €2bn (£1.6bn) higher in the short-term and its boss, Michael O'Leary, said airfares would have to rise by "double-digits" to help cover the cost.

But the firm said that was unlikely to be enough and it is looking into pay freezes. Unite, the union representing Ryanair staff, said it had not been told of "any such proposals".

O'Leary also said the company would slow down hiring as airline's costs rise.

The airline said its pre-tax profits fell by 16% to €2.4bn during the six months to the end of September, largely due to fuel costs jumping by 15%.

The company said that although 80% of its fuel bill had been "hedged" – in effect, bought in advance at fixed prices – the cost of the remainder was elevated.

O'Leary reiterated forecasts from earlier this year Ryanair would "need a 20% fare increase" to cover the cost of jet fuel.

"I'm not sure we'll get to 20%," he said. "But we're certainly looking at double-digit fare increases across Europe from all airlines in 2027."

Aviation fuel prices have surged this year as a result of the US-Israel war with Iran, which has dramatically reduced the supply of refined products coming from the Gulf and increased competition for those produced elsewhere.

Ryanair also said it was weighing up whether to freeze pay, as multi-year wage deals with unions come to to an end. The policy could be implemented from April next year.

Oliver Richardson, national officer at Unite, said the union "hasn't been advised of any such proposals and we have a multi-year pay deal in place which covers next year. A number of Unions across Europe have the same".

He said: "Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured."

Ryanair also said it would increase its use of artificial intelligence within its back office and support functions.

Meanwhile, Ryanair has cut back on winter flights and said on Monday there would be more to come. It said this was happening across the airline industry, particularly with short-haul carriers.

O'Leary said: "We believe those cuts will continue into the summer of 2027. Over the medium term, we expect short-haul capacity will remain constrained out to the early 2030s."

articles.title: Thousands evacuated as India braces for second cyclone in a week
articles.summary: Cyclone Murasu expected to hit near Ongole late Monday with wind speeds of 100-110km/h, Meteorological Department says.
articles.body:
Authorities in India’s southern state of Andhra Pradesh have begun evacuating residents from low-lying coastal areas as Cyclone Murasu bears down on a region still recovering from a deadly cyclone last week.

About 2,000 people had been evacuated by Monday, Prakhar Jain, managing director of the Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority, told the Reuters news agency. “We are planning to evacuate some 30,000 people,” he said.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) said the cyclone was likely to cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast between Nellore and Narsapur near the town of Ongole from 11:30pm (18:00 GMT) on Monday to 4am on Tuesday (22:30 GMT on Monday).

“It is very likely to … cross south Andhra Pradesh coast as a severe cyclonic storm with wind speeds of around 100 to 110 kilometres per hour [60 to 70 miles per hour],” IMD said, projecting gusts of 120km/h (75mph).

Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu directed officials to prepare for the cyclone. He said estimates suggested that 6,000 to 8,000 electrical poles could be damaged, posing a “severe threat to power supply”.

Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan wrote on X that the cyclone was set to have a severe impact on Nellore, Prakasam, Bapatla and Krishna districts.

Six National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams and seven State Disaster Response Force teams have been deployed in advance, Jain said, according to the IANS news agency. Three of the NDRF teams were sent from neighbouring Tamil Nadu, the ANI news agency reported.

In Nellore district, Collector Himanshu Shukla urged fishermen not to go to sea and ordered officials in coastal areas to remain at their posts.

Schools have been closed in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Odisha with rain expected to continue over parts of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Odisha and Chhattisgarh until Wednesday even as the storm weakens, according to ETV Bharat.

Murasu is expected to be less intense than Cyclone Arnab, which struck the same coastline on Wednesday, killing six people and destroying dozens of homes and crops.

articles.title: Oracle founder Larry Ellison believes America is on right track with AI, he sees robots taking jobs, and says what is needed is right taxation system
articles.summary: Larry Ellison believes AI can make everyone wealthier.
articles.body: ​Larry Ellison believes AI can make everyone wealthier. The Oracle co-founder and chief technology officer says robots will take over some jobs, but argues that greater productivity and changes to taxation could help spread the resulting wealth. Speaking at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, he described a future in which automation reduces the cost of goods and services while US governments collect revenue from the value machines create.​“We need to change from taxing human labour to taxing value added,” he said. “So when the robots add value, all that value that the robots add is taxed, and we could have universal high income.” His argument links AI’s economic benefits to how governments distribute them, with less reliance on taxing people’s work.​How robots could reduce costs while replacing some jobs​Ellison rejected the suggestion that AI would eventually replace everyone, calling that prediction “kind of nonsensical”. However, he acknowledged that automation would displace some workers, pointing to rideshare services as an example.​He argued that better tools could also allow people to accomplish more. In the supplied account of his remarks, he cited robotic surgeons and aircraft autopilot systems to illustrate how technology can change work and improve productivity.​To explain the potential effect on prices, Ellison described a hypothetical house built entirely by robots. If human labour previously accounted for 80% of its cost, he suggested, automating construction could substantially reduce that expense. The example illustrated his prediction about cheaper production; it was not a reported result from an actual housing project.​How would universal high income work​Ellison’s proposal centres on taxing the economic value generated by automation and using that revenue to support people’s incomes. Universal basic income generally means regular payments intended to cover essential living costs. The universal high income he described would go further, relying on AI-driven productivity to support higher living standards even as machines do more of the work.​He also referred to economist Milton Friedman’s negative income tax proposal, describing it as a “reverse income tax”. Broadly, such a system pays people whose incomes fall below a specified threshold. Ellison’s comments outlined a possible direction for taxation rather than a detailed policy. The supplied excerpts do not specify tax rates, payment amounts, or eligibility rules.​He acknowledged that the transition would take more than a decade, with robots gradually taking on more tasks people don't want to do.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nuclear radiation in Russia, Ukraine? No, just hacked warning alerts
articles.summary: Warnings startle people in Ukraine, but authorities say they cleared up the confusion in under an hour.
articles.body:
Ukraine and Russia have accused each other of hacking into systems used to send out emergency alerts to citizens, raising fears of a new escalation of digital and psychological warfare tactics.

The systems’ apps sent out radiation alerts on Sunday and Monday to civilians before officials issued public clarifications.

The fake threats began on the same day as a localised ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Kherson region came to an end on Sunday. The truce, which the United States said was brokered by first lady Melania Trump, is the longest so far in Russia’s more than four-year war on Ukraine. The ceasefire lasted for six days, during which humanitarian aid and evacuations were allowed in the Russian-occupied town of Olekshy.

Al Jazeera’s Audrey Macalpine, reporting from Kyiv, said many people in Ukraine now expect renewed fighting along the front lines.

Here’s what we know about the fake notifications:

Ukraine’s Air Force said late on Sunday that users of its Air Alert app, which warns people of incoming air attacks, received fake warnings of nuclear and chemical threats to areas in and around Kyiv.

Users were also warned of potential street combat and told that Russia’s hypersonic Oreshnik missile had been deployed.

“The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the Ukrainian Air Force said on Telegram.

“There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”

Ukraine’s Center for Strategic Communications blamed Russia. In a post on X, the agency pointed to the use of the Russian language in one of the fake messages. The Ukrainian government said a separate app created for the capital city was working normally.

The fake alerts came just after 10pm (20:00 GMT), startling a lot of people, Macalpine reported.

“Even the speakers here in the centre of the city rang out warnings of these attacks,” she said. “But most people here understood within at least half an hour that this was some kind of hacking attack.”

Hours later on Monday morning, similar announcements came from Russia’s Ministry of Civil Defence, Emergencies and Disaster Relief, which said its warnings app came under a “massive cyberattack” and wrongly warned users of imminent drone attacks. The ministry did not name any suspects but said the alerts spread “false information”.

Media reports said the hackers warned Russians that “nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [Ukrainian drones] had been launched on all regions” of the country. The alerts also instructed people to “urgently” stock up on food for three weeks and to hide.

This appears to be the first time either Ukraine’s or Russia’s official alert apps have been hacked.

However, cyberwarfare has long been a major part of the countries’ previous confrontations.

Russian hackers have attacked Ukraine’s election systems in the past and in January 2022 attacked Ukrainian government and banking sites. Cyberwarfare tactics have only intensified since February 2022 when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In late 2023, the Russian hacker group Sandworm took the private telecommunications network Kyivstar offline, disrupting notifications for days.

Ukrainian groups have also launched multiple cyberattacks on Russia.

The country’s volunteer-based IT Army of Ukraine was founded in the wake of Russia’s invasion specifically to engage in cyberwarfare against Russia and has reportedly targeted the Moscow Stock Exchange, Russia’s power grids and several government websites. In 2022, the Reuters news agency reported Ukrainian attackers used facial recognition software to scan the faces of dead Russian combatants and notified their families of their deaths.

Why is the threat of nuclear radiation in Ukraine significant?

Ukraine is particularly vulnerable because it has already suffered one nuclear disaster and it remains at risk due to fighting around another major nuclear plant.

In April 1986, the Chornobyl nuclear power plant , located in the then-Ukrainian Soviet Republic, exploded, releasing radioactive material. Scores of people died from the explosion itself, but thousands later developed severe health issues as a result, including thyroid cancer. Radiation was detected as far away as Sweden. It’s regarded as one of the two worst nuclear accidents in history along with the 2011 Fukushima disaster in Japan. Chornobyl remains a ghost town after its inhabitants were evacuated.

Ongoing fighting in the Ukrainian region of Zaporizhia has raised fears that the tragic story could repeat itself. Russia partly controls the region, including Enerhodar, where the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, Europe’s largest nuclear energy facility, is located.

Both sides have repeatedly launched attacks on each other’s positions with Russia targeting the Ukrainian-held provincial capital, Zaporizhzhia, and Ukraine targeting Russian-held areas, including Enerhodar.

Last week, the International Atomic Energy Agency, the United Nations nuclear watchdog, said a welder working at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant was killed in a drone attack. The head of the agency, Rafael Grossi, called for “maximum military restraint” from both sides.

articles.title: Bonnie Tyler Christmas single Love, Light and Peace to be released
articles.summary: Bonnie Tyler's last studio recording will be released as a Christmas single on November 13.
articles.body:
Bonnie Tyler's husband said it has "been a heartbreaking year" following her death and that he misses her "every single day".

Tyler, born Gaynor Hopkins, died in July aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this year.

The Total Eclipse of the Heart singer's last studio recording, Love, Light and Peace, will be released as a Christmas single on 13 November 2026.

Tyler's husband of 50 years, Robert Sullivan, said: "Gaynor never stopped working. She loved singing, she loved her fans, and she poured her whole heart into these songs."

Tyler was born in a Neath council house where she grew up with a love of music before being discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a Swansea club.

After finding fame she was dubbed "the female Rod Stewart" for her husky vocals, and launched a career that spanned 50 years .

In August, fans travelled to Swansea to line the streets as a celebration of life service was held for Tyler at Swansea Minster.

"The only time she ever had off was during Covid, and even then she was still on Zoom doing interviews all the time," said Sullivan.

"Between live shows she would stop by David Mackay's studio to work on all these new songs.

"I know she would want people to hear them, and I am so proud of everything she left behind."

After her last record contract expired, Tyler began self-releasing songs, with Yes I Can released on New Year's Day 2025, and then Only Love in March 2026, shortly before she became unwell.

Love, Light and Peace was written by Chrissie Hammond and 2026 Songwriters Hall of Fame inductee Terry Britten. It was produced by Britten and David Mackay, who both worked with Tyler at the start of her career.

Tyler first worked with Britten in 1977, when he played guitar on her debut album, The World Starts Tonight.

Nearly 50 years later, he returned as a writer and producer of the last song she recorded.

November would have seen Tyler in the middle of her Jubilee Tour across Europe, celebrating 50 years since her song Lost in France broke her into the UK Singles Chart in 1976.

articles.title: As aid situation worsens, displaced Sudanese worry about warnings of famine
articles.summary: Sudan’s displaced people now face a mounting food crisis, with warnings of famine.
articles.body:
The sound of gunfire forced 50-year-old Aisha Adam to flee her home in the al-Kalakla neighbourhood of Khartoum days after war erupted in Sudan between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on April 15, 2023.

She went to the neighbouring city of Omdurman, but fighting followed her and in May 2023, Adam had to find a new refuge. It brought her to a camp for internally displaced people (IDPs) in Port Sudan, on the country’s Red Sea coast, where she lives with her orphaned grandson and nephew.

“Amid the clashes, I left with my grandson for the bus station, intending to travel to Wad Madani in Gezira state, south of Khartoum. But I found a bus heading to Port Sudan and boarded it, even though all I knew about the city was that it was safe,” she told Al Jazeera.

The fighting between the SAF and the RSF has killed as many as 200,000 people, according to aid workers. The war has also displaced 13 million people and led to famine in parts of the country.

After Adam was forced to move to Port Sudan, she initially stayed at a shelter for IDPs in the centre of the city. In June, she and others were relocated to a displacement centre on the outskirts of the city.

Accommodation was allocated according to household size. Adam was given a tent to share with the two children under her care, and shared a boundary with two other families.

“At the first shelter, I received some assistance from organisations, other agencies and even ordinary people. But things are different here. The aid we receive has decreased significantly, so I had to try to find work to avoid starving to death,” she said.

Adam’s struggle to feed the two children comes as Sudan faces deepening food shortages. In a joint statement released on October 27, the United States Department of State warned of the deterioration in food availability and the risk of famine in the coming months.

“Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security. The risk of famine in the coming months, as warned by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, needs urgent action,” the statement said.

Fatima is experiencing the real-life consequences highlighted in the report, as finding food becomes a daily struggle. Humanitarian assistance over the past six months has been limited, and she recalls receiving aid on only three occasions. Once, she received 550,000 Sudanese pounds ($59.13) in cash. Another time, she was given 12kg of flour. At the last distribution, she received personal hygiene supplies for women.

“I have no choice but to work. There is no one I can rely on. My two sons are missing, and I do not know where they are, while my other son died before the war began,” she said.

Adam leaves her accommodation early in the morning and heads to a nearby market, where she makes and sells zalabia, a traditional Sudanese fried pastry, alongside tea and coffee. Some days she makes a profit; on others, she loses money.

“I do not know how to calculate my profit. But as soon as I finish selling the zalabia, I go to buy the ingredients … for the next day: 3kg of flour for 21,000 pounds ($2.25), 2 litres of oil for 22,000 pounds ($2.36) and three bags of charcoal for 9,000 pounds ($0.97),” she told Al Jazeera.

Adam says the money left after buying these supplies is often insufficient to provide a meal for herself and the two children in her care. A kilogramme of lentils, one of the cheapest food items available to her, costs 16,000 pounds ($1.72). Meat is no longer on her shopping list, and her diet now consists mainly of lentils and rice.

“Fortunately, aid organisations have been providing water for the past five days. Before that, I used to buy 18 litres for 1,500 pounds ($0.16). Sometimes I did not have the money and had to borrow it,” she said.

Adam says her priority is to keep her small business running. It helps her put food on the table while helping her cope with the pain of not knowing what happened to her two missing sons.

“The important thing is that we eat, even if it is only lentils and water, with nothing else. But my greatest fear is that we will fall ill, because we have no money for treatment,” she said.

Her struggle reflects the wider food crisis facing millions in Sudan. On October 22, 2026, the World Food Programme (WFP) announced that funding shortages had forced it to cut monthly food assistance to displaced people, affecting about 900,000 people.

Meanwhile, some 19.5 million people across the country face acute hunger, including five million experiencing emergency levels of food shortages. The risk of famine persists in several hunger hotspots, particularly in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, the WFP says.

Esraa Mohammed, supervisor of the al-Suraiha 8 IDP camp in al-Obeid, says displaced families are facing severe shortages of humanitarian assistance and lack even the most basic necessities.

“We have 450 registered displaced people in the camp, in addition to 40 newly arrived people who have not yet been added to the official records,” she told Al Jazeera. “Most arrive wearing torn clothes after their journeys, with nothing to protect them from the sun or rain, and without even a single meal.”

Mohammed says some organisations provide food assistance, including about 400ml of cooking oil per person and 250gm of peas per person. Another organisation distributes lentils, flour, oil and salt.

But these supplies are insufficient to sustain her family for a month, forcing her and other displaced Sudanese to look for casual work to make ends meet. Sometimes they find work; at other times, they go to bed without food.

“There are 100 children in the camp, 30 of whom are suffering from severe acute malnutrition. They also urgently need clothes to protect them from harsh weather conditions and cover their small bodies,” she said.

Mohammed added that some displaced people arriving from South Kordofan had told her they were forced to eat tree leaves while fleeing their homes because they feared being killed by the RSF, following reports of civilians being murdered, detained or raped by fighters from the group.

Ahmed Ismail, an expert on the United Nations and NGOs, describes the humanitarian situation in Sudan as extremely serious, with the basic needs of the population far exceeding the support being provided.

“Sudan is facing a complex crisis involving famine, displacement, the collapse of health services, the destruction of livelihoods and serious violations against civilians,” he told Al Jazeera.

Humanitarian monitoring had indicated an increase in civilian deaths, including those linked to difficulties accessing food, healthcare and shelter, as well as casualties from attacks and violations, including drone strikes .

“When assistance declines, the most vulnerable families are deprived of food and medicine, increasing the risk of death among children, women and older people, particularly in conflict and displacement areas,” Ismail said.

Continued reductions in aid, alongside escalating violations and restrictions on humanitarian access, could turn the crisis into an even wider catastrophe, he warned.

“Denying the severity of conditions in some areas did not change the reality of the suffering experienced by civilians,” he said.

articles.title: Jailed PKK founder Ocalan moved to new section of Turkish island prison
articles.summary: Improving prison conditions for Abdullah Ocalan has been a key Kurdish demand in push to end PKK-Turkiye conflict.
articles.body:
Turkiye has moved the jailed founder of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), Abdullah Ocalan, to a newly-built section of the island prison where he has been held for 27 years, pro-Kurdish legislators said as they urged Ankara to speed up the stalled peace process.

Mithat Sancar, a member of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM) delegation that regularly visits Ocalan, confirmed the transfer on Saturday in an interview with the Kurdish television channel Medya Haber TV.

He said the move “necessitates an acceleration of the (peace) process”, which he said had been paused for two months. “The process cannot proceed with unilateral expectations and demands,” he said.

Fellow DEM politician Pervin Buldan said on Sunday that Ocalan himself had announced the transfer, but played down its significance.

“This new facility is part of the prison; it is not somewhere outside the prison,” she said, according to the AFP news agency. “The question of status cannot be defined solely by Mr Ocalan having moved to this location.”

Erbil-based broadcaster Kurdistan24 described the facility as a new house built for Ocalan on Imrali island. It said the move was seen as part of preparations to give him a more active role in the peace process. Better prison conditions for Ocalan have been a key Kurdish demand.

The PKK was founded in 1978 by Ocalan and others, initially fighting for an independent Kurdish state, before shifting its demands to autonomy and greater rights for Turkiye’s Kurds, who make up an estimated 15 to 20 percent of the population. The group launched an armed campaign against the Turkish state in 1984 and is designated a “terrorist” organisation by Turkiye, the United States and the European Union.

The conflict has killed more than 40,000 people . Ocalan has been held on Imrali, in the Sea of Marmara, since his capture in 1999.

In February last year, Ocalan called on the PKK to disband and disarm and the group announced its dissolution that May. Turkiye’s parliament adopted a law offering limited amnesty for PKK fighters in August and the PKK leadership has repeatedly demanded Ocalan’s release as part of the process.

articles.title: Suspected cyberattacks trigger supermarket fridge failures across Europe
articles.summary: Temperature increases have been reported in dozens of store cooling systems , weeks after a similar attack in France.
articles.body:
Suspected cyberattacks have triggered temperatures to rise in grocery store refrigeration systems in a growing number of countries across Europe.

Overnight temperature spikes were recorded in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden. On Monday, retailers and authorities pointed to alleged cyberattacks that underscored the vulnerability of systems that once largely operated mechanically.

The head of ⁠⁠⁠⁠Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, confirmed on Monday to the Reuters news agency that the centre ⁠⁠⁠⁠is responding to ⁠⁠⁠⁠multiple incidents affecting store cooling systems.

“We have in recent weeks … identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” he said.

The temperature of freezers in several Swedish stores rose suddenly overnight, store operators ICA and Coop said, while Swedish retailer Axfood said freezers at a distribution centre for home delivery of groceries in the Gothenburg area were hacked.

SuperValu, Ireland’s third-largest supermarket chain, ⁠⁠⁠⁠said a specific model of refrigeration systems has been affected by a “cyber incident” at 13 of its 223 ⁠⁠⁠⁠stores.

The Belga news agency reported overnight temperature increases at dozens of ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Ahold Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg. They were blamed on a cyberattack, according to the chief ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠executive ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠of refrigeration company,⁠ ⁠⁠⁠Sabcobel.

Stephan Moelans said the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.

Also in Belgium, five Spar shops had their fridge systems attacked, said a spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates the franchise system.

In Estonia, at least one supermarket chain was affected, technology supplier Kitman Coldtech told public broadcaster ERR.

“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” Kitman’s CEO Jann Mutso said, without naming the affected chain.

Ahold Delhaize reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police last month.

The cyberattack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets in France raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F), spoiling food and causing fires at several stores.

One Swedish store said in a social media post on Monday that the temperature of its refrigerators and freezers had been set to the same temperature as during the cyberattack in France.

“We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems,” a spokesperson for privately held ICA told Reuters in an email.

Kitman’s Mutso also said that temperatures at the Estonian chain were set to 50 degrees Celsius (122F).

Privately-held retailer Coop told Swedish daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents.

There has been no claim of responsibility for Monday’s attack, nor the one earlier in France.

However, the incidents help to increase concern regarding hybrid warfare stemming from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran-United States war.

European states have blamed Moscow for a growing number of incidents affecting infrastructure, including via cyberattacks, in recent months. Russia has repeatedly denied involvement in any sabotage or hybrid warfare operations.

European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said the attacks were “a deliberate attempt ⁠to disrupt” EU food supplies and undermine public ‌confidence.

“These incidents show that cyberattacks ⁠can disrupt services, affect ⁠businesses and directly affect citizens’ ⁠daily lives”, a ⁠European Commission spokesperson ⁠said, stressing the importance of strengthening ‌cybersecurity across the bloc.

A spokesperson for The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium told Al Jazeera that the rising number of cyberattack incidents, especially those resulting from the targeted use of AI, is an evolving trend.

However, they added, “we may never be able to identify … who is behind this attack”.

articles.title: Four Americans and 1 Canadian among the 69 dead in Spain’s train crash
articles.summary: Four Americans and one Canadian were among the 69 people killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.
articles.body: MADRID — Four Americans and one Canadian were among the 69 people killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said. So far, 66 of the dead have been identified, authorities said late Sunday. Most of those killed in the crash last Wednesday when a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks were Spanish nationals. Other foreigners among the fatalities who have been identified include one each from France, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Portugal, Tunisia and the Czech Republic. Authorities said three persons remained missing — two Australians and one Japanese. The crash in the province of Toledo came just nine months after another collision farther south on the same Madrid-Seville line killed 46 people. The collisions have shaken confidence in the Spanish rail network long hailed for its speed and safety. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has pledged an investigation and improvements to restore trust in the system that carried some 45 million travelers last year, including millions of tourists. The crash happened one month before a Nov. 29 general election in which Sánchez is seeking to extend his eight-year premiership. He is now facing questions about the safety of the railways and investments under his governments in Spanish infrastructure.

articles.title: Council confident Whitesands flood scheme is on firm legal ground
articles.summary: It comes after concerns were raised about using common good land on the Whitesands in Dumfries.
articles.body:
A council has said it is confident of its legal position after concerns were raised about land being used for a £68m flood protection scheme.

Dumfries and Galloway Council (DGC) said it wanted to "set out the facts" about the use of common good land - owned by the local authority for the benefit of the community - as part of the project.

It comes after calls for greater transparency after it was found to have "failed at the most basic level" in its response to freedom of information (FOI) requests about the scheme.

The council said it had taken legal advice and was confident that tackling the flood risk in the area was "consistent with its duty to protect and advance the common good".

Call for 'transparency' over £68m flood scheme information

Council's flood scheme request approach 'entirely unacceptable'

Earlier this year, the man behind the FOI requests told the BBC he believed there had been a "catalogue of errors" in the handling of the scheme.

Mike Sutherland said the Local Government (Scotland) Act 1973 required the council to seek court approval to use common good land before work got under way.

He asked for information about the use of common good land and whether it had petitioned the courts for a change of use.

His call was backed by Conservative MSP Craig Hoy who urged the council to answer questions about the scheme "fully, openly and transparently".

The council has now said it was "neither appropriating nor disposing of the land" and would continue to manage it on behalf of the community.

"The land will remain in council ownership and continue to be held as common good land throughout the project and after completion," it said.

"Following completion of the works, it will remain within the public realm and retain its status as open public space."

It said that, in 2014, the council's common good sub-committee had approved the use of the land for the scheme and that legal advice was that it had acted appropriately.

"Where common good land is involved, the Whitesands Project will help protect, improve and safeguard it for future generations," it said.

"The council considers that addressing the long-standing risk of flooding is consistent with its duty to protect and advance the common good."

It added that it also intended to work towards tackling recent criticism from the Scottish Information Commissioner abouts its responses to FOI requests about the project.

"In response to the commissioner's decisions, we have now carried out additional searches for information and issued our responses to the relevant requester," it said.

"We will continue to co-operate with the commissioner's requirements."

It added that it realised people had "different views" about the project but it would continue to provide "clear and accurate information" about the work and what it would deliver for people and businesses in the town.

Town's £68m flood scheme cleared to progress

articles.title: Charles left without umbrella in rainstorm fit for a king
articles.summary: King Charles flung up his hands in despair as he was caught in a tropical rainstorm in ​Antigua, while his wife Queen Camilla strolled off with the ‌only available umbrella.
articles.body: SAINT GEORGE, Antigua and Barbuda — King Charles flung up his hands in despair as he was caught in a tropical rainstorm in ​Antigua, while his wife Queen Camilla strolled off with the ‌only available umbrella. The couple’s Caribbean tour has been dominated by the debate over Britain’s role in the slave trade, but it was the sight of the soaked monarch ​which made headlines this weekend. As the rain hammered down on ​Charles, 77, he was seen gesturing and turning round to ⁠try to attract the attention of someone who might help, while Camilla ​was shielded from the downpour. Locals taking part in the Antigua and Barbuda ​independence day parade did not flinch as they were lashed by the storm. Charles was eventually given an umbrella and was seen joking about his experience with Prime ​Minister Gaston Browne. “I think I’m about to grow watercress on my suit,” ​he said in a video posted on the royal family’s Instagram account. It is not ‌the ⁠first time the frustration of the famously short-fused monarch has been captured in public. Not long after he became king in 2022 in an incident which went viral on social media, he reacted grumpily when a pen ​leaked ink onto ​his hand at ⁠an event in Northern Ireland. “Oh God, I hate this,” he cursed. “I can’t bear this bloody thing... every stinking ​time,” he continued. He has since made fun of himself, ​quipping ⁠at a subsequent event, “I’m hoping that my pen is going to work. It doesn’t usually.” He is due to make a speech to Commonwealth leaders on ⁠Tuesday. ​Since becoming king, he has expressed sorrow ​for the suffering caused by slavery without crossing a line that Britain has long resisted: an ​apology.

articles.title: A family in London kept a strange stuffed animal head under a bed for years; experts identified it as one of just three known mounted Tasmanian tiger heads, now estimated to fetch £30,000 to £50,000 at auction
articles.summary: A family living in London has discovered a rare mounted taxidermy head of an extinct thylacine, also known as the Tasmanian tiger, inside a box stored
articles.body: A family living in London has discovered a rare mounted taxidermy head of an extinct thylacine, also known as the Tasmanian tiger, inside a box stored under a bed. The specimen had been forgotten in storage for decades. It is one of only three known mounted thylacine heads in the world. It is due to be sold at Auctioneum in Bath, where experts expect it to sell for between £30,000 and £50,000. The discovery comes after the same auction house sold another mounted thylacine head. That earlier specimen had plastic googly eyes attached by a previous owner. It was bought at an antiques market for £50 before being sold to collector James Cranfield for £50,000. The price reached £60,000 after buyer fees were added.Discovery under a London bedThe family contacted Auctioneum after seeing news reports about the earlier thylacine sale. They brought in a wooden box that had been kept under a bed in their London home for years. The family had not known what was inside or how valuable it might be. Auction house staff gave the newly discovered specimen the nickname "Trevor" while they examined and valued it. X-ray scans showed that the animal's original skull was still intact inside the taxidermy mount. Experts then checked and confirmed the specimen's authenticity. It was also officially added to the global database of known surviving thylacine remains.Rarity of the Tasmanian tigerThe thylacine was a meat-eating marsupial that once lived in Australia, Tasmania, and New Guinea. The animals disappeared from mainland Australia around 2,000 years ago, but a population survived in Tasmania until Europeans settled there. Heavy hunting, encouraged by government payments for killing the animals, along with habitat loss and diseases brought in by other animals, caused their numbers to fall quickly during the 19th and early 20th centuries. The last known living thylacine, named Benjamin, died in captivity at Hobart Zoo in Tasmania in September 1936. Records held by scientific institutions and collected by Auctioneum show that only 756 physical thylacine specimens are known to exist worldwide. Of these, just 101 are taxidermy mounts. Complete mounted heads are even rarer and make up the smallest group of surviving specimens.Authentication and market demandUnlike the earlier discovery, the newly found head is in good condition and has not been changed or altered. Andrew Stowe of Auctioneum spoke about the discovery process during the previous sale. He explained how surprising it was to find such rare items in private homes in the UK. Speaking about the rarity of these mounted specimens, Stowe said: "It is unbelievably rare. To find a complete item like this is almost unheard of, especially here in the UK." Auctioneum representatives said the newly discovered specimen had gone through a full scientific check before being offered for sale. "This one, it's already been authenticated, it's already been added to the database. It's the only one to have come up to have been done properly," Stowe told ABC News.Details of the upcoming saleThe specimen is listed for sale at Auctioneum's upcoming auction on Thursday, 26 November. The auction is expected to attract interest from international institutions, private collectors, and natural history museums. This is partly because strict laws limit the export and sale of historic animal remains. The very small number of thylacine specimens available on the open market also makes the item especially valuable. Auctioneum expects the final sale price to reach or go above its estimated value of £30,000 to £50,000.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: A former campaign worker for Michigan politician Abdul El-Sayed is among 12 pro-Palestinian activists indicted by federal prosecutors over an alleged conspiracy involving threats, vandalism and intimidation targeting members of the state's Jewish community and University of Michigan officials.Mariam Odeh, 24, who worked for El-Sayed's Michigan Senate campaign for two weeks in 2024, was among eight people initially charged in the case. Four more alleged co-conspirators were indicted on October 30, taking the total number of defendants to 12, according to federal prosecutors.Odeh was paid nearly $750 for her work on El-Sayed's campaign, The Detroit News reported in June, citing campaign records and a spokesperson for the candidate. She left the campaign on April 15, 2024, after working as an hourly employee.According to an indictment unsealed by federal prosecutors, the group allegedly orchestrated a campaign of threats and vandalism in an attempt to force the University of Michigan to cut ties with Israel. The alleged targets included former university president Santa Ono, Regent Jordan Acker, other university officials, law enforcement personnel and businesses perceived to have links with Israel.The latest indictment, which brings the number of accused to 12, alleges that members of the group vandalised properties, spray-painted anti-Israel slogans and threw containers containing noxious substances into residential properties.Prosecutors also alleged that the activists discussed kidnapping and firebombing potential targets, including a pro-life centre.Odeh was allegedly involved in vandalising a Rolls-Royce Solutions America Inc. building in Detroit in 2024. The group allegedly padlocked the building's doors and spray-painted slogans including "FREE PALESTINE" and "LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA" outside the premises.According to The New York Post, Odeh was also among activists accused of targeting the homes of university board members, planting fake corpses on lawns and spray-painting anti-Israel messages outside the home of the university's then-president.The alleged attacks included breaking windows and throwing jars containing noxious chemicals into family homes. The group also allegedly posted footage of the incidents on social media, warning victims that "you cannot hide", the report said.Odeh was charged in June with one count of conspiracy to transmit threats in interstate and foreign commerce. The charge carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison.Who are the four newly indicted?The four additional defendants named in the October 30 indictment are Henry David MacKeen-Shapiro, 23, of Detroit; Aaron Hunter Vonbargen, 25, of Ypsilanti; Joseph Mark Fisher, 23; and Srishti Tarana Sharma, 23, of Canada.They face charges related to the alleged conspiracy to transmit threats, while Sharma also faces a charge of destruction of property.MacKeen-Shapiro and Vonbargen appeared in federal court in Detroit on October 30 and were released on $10,000 unsecured bonds. Two of the four newly indicted defendants are still at large, prosecutors said.The eight people charged in the initial indictment include Zainab Hakim, who prosecutors have described as the alleged ringleader, her sister Amatullah Hakim, Paige Feyock, Ahmet Korkaya, Jonathan Zou, Alexander Sepulveda, Odeh and Colin Weger.US Attorney Jerome Gorgon said the alleged attempts to intimidate members of the Jewish community and government officials would be pursued by federal authorities.You use AI every day.
